text: Time to build ask dot py for real. This lesson walks through every piece in order: parsing a command-line argument, wrapping the API call in a class, handling the failures that actually happen over a network, and testing the parts that don't need a live connection.

Three files, deliberately small. ask dot py holds both the command-line logic and the API client. requirements dot txt pins the two dependencies. test underscore ask dot py stays separate, so the tests can import from ask dot py without running it as a script.

argparse is the standard-library way to build a CLI. Making prompt a required positional argument means if someone runs this with no prompt at all, argparse prints a usage message and exits on its own — no extra code needed from you.

This is the exact same pattern from lesson seventeen: a class that holds configuration, here the API key, in init, and exposes one clear method. resp dot raise for status, from lesson twenty-four, turns a bad HTTP status into an exception immediately instead of silently returning garbage.

A real CLI tool shouldn't dump a raw Python traceback at a user. Catching the specific requests exceptions from chapter five and printing a one-line message to stderr, with a non-zero exit code so other programs can detect the failure, is what separates a script from a tool.

unittest dot mock dot patch replaces requests dot post with a fake version for the duration of the test, so it runs instantly and never touches the real network — exactly the kind of test lesson thirty-one's checklist called for.
Argument parsing, a client class, real error handling, and tests that don't need the network — that's ask dot py. Next lesson: running the finished tool for real, and wrapping up the whole capstone.
